node-1.label: A 59-year-old female had a 2-year history of difficulty understanding spoken language; she described conversation as sounding like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas.

node-2.label: 59-year-old right-handed female with 12 years of education and a 5-year history of well-controlled hypertension.

node-3.label: She reported spoken conversation sounded like noise or buzzing, especially in crowded areas; she could not understand spoken questions during the interview but comprehended and responded correctly through lip reading or gestural cues; she struggled to understand television dialogue but could follow foreign movies with Korean subtitles; environmental noises like doorbells and ringing phones were perceived and responded to appropriately; a hearing aid prescribed by an otolaryngology clinic did not improve her comprehension.

node-4.label: One year after symptom onset, she began making errors in simple mathematics and her spoken language comprehension declined significantly, though she could still read and write; her writing style became rough with frequent spelling errors; she occasionally forgot things but it did not impact daily life; she had trouble recalling names of familiar neighbors but recognized them visually; her demeanor and personal relationships remained unaffected.

node-5.label: On examination, she scored 17 out of 30 on the Mini-Mental State Examination, with specific deficits in calculation, recall, and language; neurological examination was unremarkable except for mild rigidity in the right upper extremity; the Korean version of the Western Aphasia Battery showed fluent spontaneous speech with phonemic paraphasia and mild neurogenic stuttering, severe impairments in comprehension and repetition, and mild impairments in visual confrontational naming and word generation; she could read aloud and understand written words and sentences, and communicate in writing with some literal errors; audiological examination revealed mild bilateral sensorineural hearing loss with pure-tone thresholds of 30 dB in the left ear and 35 dB in the right ear within the 500-2,000 Hz range, speech audiometry thresholds of 50 dB in the left ear and 60 dB in the right ear, and speech discrimination abilities of 32% at 80 dB in the left ear and 20% at 85 dB in the right ear; brainstem auditory evoked potential responses were normal; she recognized six out of eight nonverbal animal sounds and correctly matched four out of six songs to their written titles; neuropsychological testing showed below-normal performance on the Korean version of the Boston Naming Test, ideomotor praxis, Rey figure-copying test, calculation, finger naming, and the semantic subtest of the controlled oral association word recall test; in a Navon figure task, she recognized only small letters; she had difficulty naming famous people but could describe the occupations of some she could not name; routine laboratory tests showed no evidence of comorbid disease.

attrs.why: New expert analyses and imaging biomarkers (FDG-PET bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism, MRI bilateral temporal atrophy, PIB-PET diffuse cortical amyloid deposition) strongly support a neurodegenerative process underlying the progressive aphasia/dementia. Combined with existing evidence of progressive spoken comprehension loss, language/math decline, and MMSE/WAB/neuropsychological deficits, confidence increases from 0.78 to 0.92.

Central auditory dysfunction remains supported by speech-as-noise, ineffective hearing aid, disproportionate speech discrimination loss with normal BAEP, but new imaging evidence of neurodegenerative dementia provides a stronger alternative explanation for the progressive language/cognitive decline. Expert analyses state central auditory dysfunction may contribute but does not explain progression, so confidence decreases from 0.62 to 0.55.

Peripheral hearing loss remains mild on audiogram, but new expert analyses reiterate hearing aid ineffective and intact environmental sound responses, and neurodegenerative imaging better explains the progressive symptoms; peripheral hearing loss is unlikely to be the primary cause. Confidence decreases from 0.12 to 0.10.

Hypertension remains a vascular risk factor, but new imaging shows a neurodegenerative pattern (temporoparietal hypometabolism, temporal atrophy, amyloid deposition) and no focal vascular lesions. Expert analyses note vascular cognitive impairment lacks focal evidence, so confidence decreases from 0.10 to 0.05.

node-11.label: MRI shows bilateral temporal lobe mild atrophy, left predominant

node-12.label: PIB-PET shows diffuse cortical amyloid deposition, especially in temporoparietal-occipital regions, increased

attrs.why: PIB-PET amyloid deposition and FDG-PET temporoparietal hypometabolism are characteristic of Alzheimer disease; combined with progressive language/cognitive decline and WAB/neuropsychological deficits, they support Alzheimer disease as the underlying cause. Confidence is 0.75 because definitive tau/pathology confirmation is lacking and the clinical syndrome is progressive aphasia, which can be atypical.

node-16.label: Logopenic variant primary progressive aphasia due to Alzheimer disease

attrs.why: The frontier 'Progressive aphasia/dementia' (node-6) is still at syndrome level and can be refined. The patient's fluent speech with phonemic paraphasia plus severe comprehension and repetition deficits, together with bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism (node-10), left-predominant temporal atrophy (node-11), and diffuse cortical amyloid on PIB-PET (node-12), all match the logopenic variant of PPA, which is the phenotype most strongly linked to underlying Alzheimer pathology (node-13).

Refines the frontier 'Progressive aphasia/dementia' (node-6). Although the patient shows some speech disruption (mild neurogenic stuttering, phonemic paraphasia in node-5), her speech remained fluent rather than agrammatic/effortful, and the diffuse amyloid burden (node-12) is not typical of frontotemporal lobar degeneration, so this remains a lower-probability refinement.

Refines the frontier 'Progressive aphasia/dementia' (node-6). The patient's spared speech fluency and preserved reading/writing (nodes 4-5) argue against the semantic variant, which classically features fluent but empty, anomic speech with loss of word meaning; the bilateral temporoparietal hypometabolism (node-10) also points away from this subtype.

Refines the frontier 'Progressive aphasia/dementia' (node-6). The only motor finding is mild right upper-extremity rigidity (node-5), which is insufficient for corticobasal syndrome, and the imaging pattern of temporoparietal hypometabolism with diffuse amyloid (nodes 10,12) is more consistent with Alzheimer pathology than corticobasal degeneration.
